text: Thank you, Mr. Reeve. Good evening, everyone. This report, as it relates to Montague Township is largely housekeeping in nature. There won't be a significant impact, but there are some amendments coming under, there are some amendments coming down the pipeline that are proposed to the Mississippi Rideau source protection plan. The source protection plan is, as council will recall, is intended to protect municipal water intakes, especially around wells and septic, around communal public wells and water intake, but also identify hazards to, as it relates to source protection across the entire Mississippi and Rideau watershed. So based on some work that said, oh, part of the policy there too, as council will recall, is that wellhead protection areas and intake protection zones have been mapped and identified around municipal intakes. So we have a couple of those in Montague Township. So the municipality of North Grenville, so the area around Kempville is, they are currently undertaking a new well and other development expansions of their municipal water treatment system. And based on that, the scientists involved in that process have identified some changes to the wellhead protection area. The wells around Kempville tie into, are part of the same aquifer as, or the broader aquifer as Merrickville's wells. So that's resulted in changes to, or proposed changes to the wellhead protection area that extends into a portion of Montague Township. So this would actually reduce the size of the wellhead protection area in Montague Township. So there are some source protection policies related to these wellhead protection areas. And based on, they've been approved by the province through the source protection plan, approved by the municipality through amendments to ROP and zoning by-law, but it required a couple of the risk management plans for certain activities happening on two sites in Montague Township. So these sites would actually be removed from the coverage if this amendment is approved. So the conservation authority staff have helpfully provided an explanatory note that's been attached to this report and also some mapping that are showing essentially the decreased scope of this wellhead protection area. So ultimately the source protection authority is looking for a concurrence from all affected municipalities that they're in agreement of that. And from our perspective, we have no reason not to provide that concurrence that it appears that this would have very little overall impact on Montague Township. There would be some changes to some of our mapping, which we capture at the next OP review. So the source protection authority has attached a resolution at the beginning of the report that they're looking for for council's concurrence. So I'll leave it there and let council discuss and direct on this. Thank you.

The first four points of the amendment are related to the introduction section of the official plan. The first point clarifies that Rosedale and Andrewsville are the primary locations for growth and hamlets within your community. The next statement is one of a series of statements that's being recommended that go into your official plan that acknowledge and recognize the Anishinaabe peoples to be the first inhabitants of Montague Township. The next point, number three, talks about the business park as being a primary focus for employment lands within the municipality. That's the change that's in this section is sort of putting the business park more front and center and hopefully getting more interest in that area for investment. The next part, again, is related to additional wording in your plan regarding indigenous communities and the duty to consult. The next section of the amendment deals with changes to the general development policies in the official plan that are found in section two. And this constitutes the majority of the changes that we're talking about. And this goes from item five to item 19. The first one deals with the economic policies. This is the preamble to the economic policies. It talks about the business park. It talks about being investment ready in the business park. It also highlights some flexibility and some tools that council may have to help promote and stimulate growth and development of the business park. I think one other thing that's included in this is the section that talks about the fact that not all growth is good growth and that some growth comes with a price tag and that there are some negative impacts associated with scattered rural residential development and that these financial issues need to be considered by council when you're reviewing development applications. The next section highlights policy changes to your energy policy. And this is to pick up on some of the new wording from the provincial policy statement, but also to recognize that larger scale energy projects are possible within Montague where in the past they weren't recognized as something that could happen. The next section is a new section that deals with secondary dwelling units. I know council's had a lot of discussion with Carl on this and we've picked up that work and this implements the provincial policy statement as well as the policies in the planning act regarding additional secondary units, both within a house as well as detached within communities. The important thing to keep in mind with this policy council is that the details for this policy will be found in your zoning by-law. This is more of a general motherhood statement and the zoning by-law will have all the details and we'll get into things such as mobile homes and things of that nature in the zoning. The next changes or even council eight through to 12 are all just editing wording requested by the ministry of Northern Development and Mines. The change in number 13 relates to consultation with first nations when you're doing archeological assessments. And it also clarifies that it's the ministry's archeological checklist that you're working from in terms of determining whether you need archeological assessment or not. The next section deals with another issue that was brought forward by the ministry of Northern Development and Mines and that's acknowledgement that there is a small pocket of karst topography. I think it's located in the Southeast corner of the municipality and these are the policies that would relate to development in that area. Karst topography is underground caves and hollowed out limestone areas. So you have to be careful when you're doing development in these areas. They are highly sensitive to impacts from septic systems in particular, which then can cause problems with wells. One of the new changes or enhancements to your official plan is a natural heritage system that shows the wetlands, and seas, rivers, lakes, things of that nature. They were all brought into one map and there were linkages and corridors that were identified. Your official plan actually went further than any other in Lanark County in identifying linkages and corridors. And this was a relatively simple undertaking for us to do because you had done so much work in the past. The one thing is, is that it wasn't clear what can and can't happen in these linkage corridors. And so we did research and it was determined that they're treated like wildlife habitat. And so that was put in there for clarification. The next one, again, is consulting the First Nations with an impact where there's native values that have been identified. The next statement is, I think, one of the more important changes that's being recommended for you, and that is to consider communal sewage treatment systems within the municipality, whether they're publicly owned or owned by a condominium or a single owner. One of the things that we've put in here is that there are implications for municipal responsibility with communal systems, and that the township is not obliged to approve the use of communal systems. However, once you do approve the use, there will be a need for a responsibility agreement and you would have to be a signature to that agreement. So the decision point is whether to do a communal system or not do a communal system. Once you decide to do it, there is a clear path and track that you have to stay on. The next section, 19, is the new section of the plan. We've brought all of the policies related to the Rideau Canal and the UNESCO World Heritage Site. We've brought them into one location so that it's going to be easier for your planner. It's going to be easier for people that are in, speaking of development in and around the canal. And this is very much a wording that's seen in all of the official plans along the entire Rideau Corridor. And they're pretty straightforward for the most part. The next section is section three of your official plan, and this is where all the land use policies are. There are some wording or name changes that are in the first few. And then there is also new policies in the natural heritage section A that relate to recognizing that in rural areas, the natural heritage features are common and that they may be a constraint and limit development. And this is said both in the rural and in the agricultural policies. There's again, a reference to the Karst topography in both 24 and 25. And then again, reiterating the policy stated above from the natural heritage systems about the fact that there are limitations to development in the rural area because of these natural heritage features. The next important section is section 28, and this is a reworking of the policies related to your business park. It clarifies the range of uses that can be permitted in that area. All those uses that are identified would meet with approval for the lands being within the source water protection zone. We also clarified the limitations because it's in that, I mean, source water intake zone. And so really the limitations are, you can't be applying organic nutrients in that area, so no manure. You can't apply pesticides in that area. And there are concerns about stormwater ponds serving large geographies. I think this helps dispel the myths that the business park is basically not being developed because it's in the source water protection zone. The source water protection zone is not a big issue for this property. And so we wanted that clarified in the policies. And again, we talk about some of the options that council can have to promote and advance the growth and development of the business park and deal with minimizing red tape. We also had discussions about potentially expanding range of options around the airport lands. We've talked about aviated related land uses as being the principle of that area, but also that new commercial and industrial development that's sensitive to the air could be considered as well. This is a policy regarding the settlement areas and it's designed to give council tools to be able to encourage and incent development in Rosedale and Andrewsville settlement areas. And again, giving council tools that were there in the past but weren't clearly spelled out in your official plan. The other thing that we've done in the official plan for settlement areas is recognize a broader range of uses including on-farm diversified uses and agriculturally related uses. And we did add in secondary dwelling units as well. So this is a more robust range of uses that can happen in your hamlets as you go forward. The other section related to the hamlets is that the plans of subdivision are going to be promoted and encouraged over the use of severances. I think severances start undermining the likelihood that you would ever get subdivision development. And so what I've done is I've borrowed from other hamlet policies that I'm familiar with that limit consents to infilling and rounding out which is a very, very common policy approach. And that generally subdivisions are the preferred form of development for hamlets. The agricultural policies are expanded with an expanded range of permitted uses particularly associated with agritourism and on-farm diversified land uses and agriculturally related uses. These are all areas detailed in the provincial policy statement that really did require clarification in your plan. And hopefully this is going to make it so that there's much less red tape for farmers that wish to diversify on-site with agriculturally related or farm produce types of advanced processing and manufacturing, typically at a small scale. It also adds in agritourism as a use as well. The final section deals with the implementation policies of your official plan. The next statement is related to the constraint and limitations that the natural heritage features may have in development in the rural area. One of the big changes council is in the next section. We have not changed the consent policies related to the number of severances. However, there is a statement in here that says that notwithstanding the policies where an application for consent has frontage on a township road that's been classified as deficient in the 2020 roads need study as amended, council shall limit the number of consents to a maximum of one new lot. That is a policy change for you. The next section deals with clarification of strip development. You did have policies that discouraged strip development but they weren't defined. And there was no sort of indication of why strip development is a bad thing. And so we did make efforts to capture the rationale for the policy at that introductory. Paragraph one new form of development that we've talked about that we're recommending is this idea of cluster lot development. This is a small little subdivision with a private road done through the consent process. And it's a policy that started in Mississippi Mills. It has been in North Granville. I don't think it's there now. They've used it up in Renfrew County a fair bit. It's actually in the new county official plan and it's also in Lanner Highlands as well. So these are the policies that are pretty much standard throughout all those documents related to cluster lot development. And then the final thing is to add the land use, the new land use schedule related to the natural heritage system mapping. Those are the contents of the amendment that were presented to you at the last meeting council. Since that time, there has been a lot of discussion throughout the county, beyond the county boundaries and involving most of the area planners regarding hydrogeologic studies. And your policies would be improved with the policy that I've included at the end of the planning report that's submitted for this evening. Myself and staff are requesting your leave to add that in, those new hydroge screening policies into this amendment to be able to have it go forward and include it in your official plan. And Reeve, that is my report. I'm very happy to answer any detailed questions that you may have going forward with the specifics of the amendment.

speaker: forbess

And I think that it's important that you have that balance. The other thing that's really important for council to appreciate is that if you have a natural feature, there are limits to what growth can, or development can encroach into that area, but it's all about the proponent doing the environmental study, having the boots on the ground, taking the environmental resource information that's figured out from an air photograph at 3,000 feet and bringing it and putting boots in the ground, and truthing what's there. And that's a really important step. And what happens through that is you get better understanding of the resource, and then you go from having 120 meter setback from a wetland down to a 30 meter setback, right? You go from having no development in the significant woodland to saying you can have six houses in this area and it's not going to have an impact, right? So the important thing is to clearly identify where the resource is, and then be able to do the studies and have clear direction on the studies so that Carl can give a report to you, and you guys can make an informed decision as to how far you need to go to protect the natural resource versus encouraging new investment. For instance, if there is a part, if somebody has, say, 100 acres that they'd like to subdivide and 15 of those acres are identified through not only through our mapping but through the environmental exercise that would have to happen, as these areas are identified really as untouchable, they need to be protected, then one thing we could do is proceed with the subdivision for the other 80 acres. To develop a private road is going to be somewhere in the neighborhood of half the cost of a road that's maintained and built up to township standards. So because the road is such a large cost component of the project, it was felt that it was important that it be a private road to be able to keep the cost down. The other thing that it does is it starts dealing with the economics of the municipality and the maintenance, right?
